newsitem.title: USA: Former NYC Mayor Dinkins declines to run again.
newsitem.headline: Former NYC Mayor Dinkins declines to run again.

text.p: Former New York City Mayor David Dinkins ended two weeks of indecision Wednesday by announcing that he would not challenge incumbent Rudolph Giuliani in the 1997 mayoral election.
Democrat Dinkins' possible entry had briefly enlivened an otherwise dull race in which Republican Giuliani enjoys a comfortable lead in opinion polls over all four potential Democratic challengers.

"I'm not running but I'm not hiding," the 69-year-old former mayor said on his "Dialogue with Dinkins" show on WLIB-AM radio. "I'm committed to doing all I can as a private citizen with a sometimes public voice to affect real and important change in our city."

Dinkins declared his interest in returning to politics Jan. 30 at the urging of close friends eager to see him back in the job he lost to Giuliani in 1993. He was the city's first black mayor, defeating incumbent Ed Koch in the 1989 Democratic primary and Giuliani in the election.
But Giuliani, a former federal prosecutor, came back to beat Dinkins four years later and has since won plaudits as New York City's crime rate dropped to the lowest levels in a generation.

Dinkins, calling Giuliani "a master of diversion," said New Yorkers lived in two worlds -- "the real world in which you and I live and work and Rudy's world." He said crime had dropped sharply in the Dinkins administration too but "the rate of brutality and misconduct by police officers has dramatically skyrocketed" since Giuliani came into office.

Dinkins called a news conference two weeks ago and insisted that, despite the polls, Giuliani was "beatable" by himself or either of the two borough presidents running in the Democratic primary. He said in his radio address that he would assist one of the Democratic candidates to win the primary and run against Giuliani but would not publicly announce his choice until Thursday.

Four Democrats will face off in the primary in September: Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger, Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer, black activist minister Al Sharpton and Brooklyn Councilman Sal Albanese.

A poll released Tuesday showed most New Yorkers plan to vote for Giuliani in November even though they do not like him very much. It showed him winning more than 50 percent of the vote against any of the potential Democratic contenders.
It also predicted Giuliani would beat Dinkins by a margin of 55 percent to 34 percent had the Democrat entered the race.

The mayor's overall approval rating is at an all-time high of 62 percent, according to the poll by Quinnipiac College in Hamden, Connecticut. But 52 percent said Giuliani did not have a "likable personality," 50 percent said he did not work well with others and 55 percent said he was not sympathetic to problems of the poor.
